q: What is the meaning of the acronym MACA?
n: MACA = Maximum Allowable Construction Area, the sum of the maximum PSO and the maximum ISA (note c of Table VIII.1). Source: 2004 Revised IRR of PD 1096 (NBCP), Rule VIII, Table VIII.1.

q: It covers the joint between two flooring materials and provides weather protection at an exterior door.
n: A threshold (saddle) is the strip fastened to the floor beneath a door. It covers the joint where two floor materials meet and gives weather protection at exterior doors. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture (Door); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 8.

q: What do you call a window on a roof?
n: A dormer is a projecting structure built out from a sloping roof, usually housing a vertical window. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture (Roof).

q: In a tropical country, which of the following would be the best window?
n: Jalousie windows have adjustable horizontal louvers. They admit breezes while shedding rain, so they suit hot-humid tropical climates where cross-ventilation is the priority. Source: Koenigsberger et al., Manual of Tropical Housing and Building; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (Window Types).

q: In feng shui, a house at a T-junction is considered unlucky because the chi coming directly from the road rushes too strongly towards it. Disregarding feng shui, why is it frowned upon for houses to be directly at a T-junction?
n: Without feng shui, the practical objection is safety. A lot at the end of a T-junction faces oncoming traffic head-on, so a vehicle that fails to turn can crash into the house. Source: De Chiara & Koppelman, Time-Saver Standards for Site Planning (lot orientation and traffic safety).

q: A device for protecting electrical appliances from lightning
n: A lightning arrester (surge arrester) diverts lightning-induced surges to ground. This protects the electrical system and the appliances connected to it. Source: Philippine Electrical Code (PEC) Part 1, Article 2.80 (Surge Arresters).

q: An occupied space between building lines and lot lines other than a yard; free, open and unobstructed by appendages from the ground upward.
n: A court is an occupied space between building lines and lot lines, other than a yard. It is open and unobstructed from the ground upward. Source: 2004 Revised IRR of PD 1096 (NBCP), Rule VIII, Sec. 804 and Definitions (Court).

q: Which Rule under the 2004 Revised IRR of the 1977 NBCP prescribes that for each type of building use/occupancy, the Allowable Maximum Total Gross Floor Area (TGFA) shall be the product of the Building Height Limit (BHL) and the Allowable Maximum Building Footprint (AMBF)?
n: Rule VII (Classification and General Requirements of All Buildings by Use or Occupancy) defines the allowable maximum TGFA as the product of the BHL and the AMBF, through Table VII.1 and Sec. 707. Source: 2004 Revised IRR of PD 1096 (NBCP), Rule VII, Table VII.1.

q: Usually mounted on a wall, it houses one or more receptacles at which current is taken to supply an electric device or appliances.
n: A convenience outlet (receptacle outlet), usually wall-mounted, houses one or more receptacles from which current is taken to supply appliances. Source: Philippine Electrical Code (PEC) Part 1, Article 1.1 (Definitions – Outlet, Receptacle).

q: What is the color coding of a Ground Wire?
n: An equipment-grounding conductor is bare, green, or green with yellow stripes. Source: Philippine Electrical Code (PEC) Part 1, Art. 2.50 (Grounding) and Art. 3.10.

q: How many chambers does a Septic Tank have?
n: A septic tank is built with at least two compartments (chambers). The first lets solids settle and digest, and the second clarifies the effluent before discharge. Source: Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines, Sec. 1002 (Septic Tanks); Philippine Sanitation Code (PD 856) IRR.

q: A concrete or masonry retaining wall at the inlet of a drain or culvert that protects the area around the inlet from scour and also directs the channel flow.
n: A wing wall is a retaining wall placed at an angle to a culvert or drain inlet or outlet. It holds back the embankment, protects the area from scour, and directs channel flow. Source: DPWH Design Guidelines, Criteria and Standards, Vol. 4 (Drainage – Culverts and Headwalls).

q: Under the NBCP, what is the minimum width of the court of a quadruplex?
n: Every court must be at least 2.00 m wide for 1- or 2-storey buildings. In cluster living units such as quadruplexes and rowhouses, this may be reduced to 1.50 m when the court is treated as a yard and the adjacent courts have at least 3.00 sqm each. Source: 2004 Revised IRR of PD 1096 (NBCP), Rule VIII, Sec. 804, item 5.

q: What is the FLARmax for the project?
n: A 4-storey multi-family building is Maximum R-3, whose FLAR is 7.10 up to 8.10 (at a 12-storey or 36.00 m BHL). The maximum is 8.10. Source: 2004 Revised IRR of PD 1096 (NBCP), Rule VII, Table VII.G.1.
scenario:
PROPOSED RESIDENTIAL CONDOMINIUM (R-3)

Statement of the problem: A property developer is erecting a 4-storey residential condominium on its property in Quezon City. The lot is 1,040 sqm in area and faces south, with a 3% slope towards a 10 m-wide RROW, and has a 40 m frontage. The building shall have 13 units per floor, each unit occupying about 33–34 sqm, with a least dimension of 4.80 m for each unit. A 200 sqm party area will be located at the roof deck. Observe proper setbacks.

Features: 52 laundry/drying cages of ±3.00 sqm with a least dimension of 1.20 m; a 33–34 sqm front lobby with stairs (least dimension 4.80 m); a 2 m-wide corridor with a fire escape at both ends on each floor; parking space at the front.

Design objective: Maximize profit.

q: What is the BHL for the project?
n: Maximum R-3 has a BHL of 12 storeys, or 36.00 m above the highest grade. Source: 2004 Revised IRR of PD 1096 (NBCP), Rule VII, Table VII.2.

q: Which section under Rule VII of the 2004 Revised IRR of the 1977 NBCP deals with parking?
n: Off-street parking slots, parking areas and loading/unloading spaces are prescribed under Sec. 707, item 4, and Table VII.4 of Rule VII. Source: 2004 Revised IRR of PD 1096 (NBCP), Rule VII, Sec. 707.

q: What is the building footprint resulting from the minimum required setbacks and the open court in the middle?
n: R-5 setbacks: front 6.00 m, sides 3.00 m, rear 3.00 m. Depth = 1,500 / 42 = 35.71 m. Width = 42 − 3 − 3 = 36 m; depth = 35.71 − 6 − 3 = 26.71 m. Buildable area = 36 × 26.71 = 961.56 sqm, less the 20 × 10 m court = 761.56 sqm. Source: 2004 Revised IRR of PD 1096 (NBCP), Rule VIII, Table VIII.2.
scenario:
PROPOSED RESIDENTIAL CONDOMINIUM (R-5)

Statement of the problem: A residential condominium will be constructed on a 1,500 sqm lot in Quezon City. It will be 12 storeys high and will have an open court, 20 m x 10 m (focal point), in the middle. Each floor will have 8 units, each unit having a depth of 7 m. Of the 8 units, 4 will be 84 sqm each and the remaining 4 units will be 70 sqm each. There will be a total of 88 units. Two (2) basement levels will serve as parking. The lot is facing west with a 2% slope towards a 20 m-wide RROW. There is a 1.20 m-wide sidewalk at the front side. The lot has a 42 m frontage. The structure must be modern yet simple. Observe proper setbacks.

q: What is the PSO of the project based on the previous item?
n: PSO = 761.56 / 1,500 = 50.8%, or about 51%. Source: 2004 Revised IRR of PD 1096 (NBCP), Rule VIII, Sec. 803.

n: For R-5 (condominiums) without firewall, Table VIII.1 sets the maximum allowable ISA at 20% of the TLA. Source: 2004 Revised IRR of PD 1096 (NBCP), Rule VIII, Table VIII.1.

q: What is the USA of the project, including the courtyard and assuming that the owner maximized the ISA allowance from the NBC?
n: TOSL = 100% − PSO = 100 − 51 = 49% (the court is open space). With the ISA at its 20% maximum, USA = 49 − 20 = 29%. Source: 2004 Revised IRR of PD 1096 (NBCP), Rule VIII, Table VIII.1 (notes c and d).

q: A type of wood product that is made out of wood particles. It includes Particle Board, MDF and Hardboard. It is heavily used in the furniture industry and a veneer of wood is usually glued onto it to give it the appearance of conventional wood.
n: Fiberboard is the family of panels made from wood fibers or particles, such as particleboard, MDF and hardboard. It is used widely for furniture, usually with a glued-on wood veneer. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 10 (Wood Panel Products); Allen & Iano, Fundamentals of Building Construction, Ch. 3.

q: If you decide to use shingles, which will you recommend for your roof sheathing?
n: Shingles are nailed to a continuous solid deck. In the humid tropics, marine (exterior-grade) plywood is recommended because its waterproof glue resists moisture and delamination. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 7 (Shingle Roofing – Sheathing); Allen & Iano, Fundamentals of Building Construction.

q: It is a small door/panel used to hide and give access to valves which are unsightly.
n: An access panel is a removable panel that hides valves, cleanouts or other concealed equipment while still allowing access to them. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines (accessibility of valves and cleanouts).

q: A cabinet sink inside the comfort room, built below or around a bathroom sink, primarily to hide exposed pipes.
n: A vanity (sink) cabinet is built below or around a lavatory to hide the exposed supply and drain pipes and to give storage. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; Time-Saver Standards for Interior Design.

q: An easily bent electrical conduit made of plastic used for the protection and routing of electrical wiring.
n: Flexible PVC conduit (flexible nonmetallic conduit) is a pliable plastic raceway that protects and routes electrical wiring. Source: Philippine Electrical Code (PEC) Part 1, Art. 3.56 (Liquidtight Flexible Nonmetallic Conduit) and Art. 3.62 (ENT).

q: A form of Indirect Lighting built into ledges, recesses, or valences in a ceiling or high on the walls of a room. It directs light up towards the ceiling and down adjacent walls.
n: Cove lighting is indirect lighting concealed in a ledge, recess or valance. It throws light up onto the ceiling and down the adjacent walls. Source: IES Lighting Handbook; Ching, Interior Design Illustrated (Lighting).

q: What is the minimum side setback required for the project?
n: Table VIII.3 requires 2.00 m side setbacks for industrial buildings along a 10.00 to 19.00 m RROW. The lot faces a 14 m RROW. Source: 2004 Revised IRR of PD 1096 (NBCP), Rule VIII, Table VIII.3.
scenario:
PROPOSED CAR REPAIR SHOP

Statement of the problem: A businessman has decided to build a car repair shop (the "Project") on his vacant 2,400 sqm lot to take advantage of the busy thoroughfare passing along the property.

Project site features: The project site, located in Caloocan City, is a rectangular inside lot with a 40.0 m wide frontage facing north and sloping down 1.5% towards a 14.0 m RROW. The property is classified as Industrial (Zone I-1) under a zoning ordinance, and the Building Official specifically prescribes a 6.0 m front setback for the property.

The concluded layout of the structure provides an 8-meter-wide unroofed driveway in the middle to separate the east wing from the west wing. Each wing shall have three divisions with the following areas:
East Wing: (a) 168.0 sqm receiving area/parking for cars to be repaired, near the entrance; (b) 168.0 sqm area for the body repair and upholstery section; (c) 168.0 sqm locker and rest area with toilet/shower facilities and a storage portion.
West Wing: (a) 168.0 sqm office/reception area with kitchenette, toilet and small storage for car parts; (b) 168.0 sqm mechanical/electrical area; (c) 168.0 sqm temporary parking.

As per the owner's requirement, the whole facility must be able to accommodate 18 cars at any given time.

q: What is the depth of the lot?
n: Depth = lot area / frontage = 2,400 / 40 = 60.00 m. Source: basic lot geometry; NBCP Rule VIII, Sec. 803.

n: Normal-weight reinforced concrete weighs about 2,400 kg per cubic meter (23.6 kN/m³). Source: NSCP 2015, Table 204-1 (Minimum Design Dead Loads); Max Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.

q: Medium & High-rise structures use High-Tensile Grade Rebars which is also classified as GRADE
n: High-tensile rebars for medium- and high-rise structures are Grade 60 (PNS 415, fy = 415 MPa). Source: PNS 49:2002 (Steel Bars for Concrete Reinforcement); NSCP 2015, Sec. 420.

q: A GRADE 60 Rebar is equivalent to
n: Grade 60 corresponds to PNS Grade 415 (minimum yield strength 415 MPa, or 60 ksi). Source: PNS 49:2002 (Steel Bars for Concrete Reinforcement).

q: These bars are not readily available, and their production is usually on a per-order basis.
n: Grade 75 (PNS 520) bars are not stocked regularly by local suppliers and are usually rolled per order. Source: PNS 49:2002; Philippine Iron and Steel Institute (PISI) product data.
